problem: Prior VLN work targets synthetic worlds or indoor room-to-room navigation. Outdoor long-range VLN datasets are hard to annotate because annotators must remember and describe whole long routes. Existing methods also match whole sentences to images, even though directional phrases cannot be grounded in a visual observation.
motivation: Human route descriptions in spatial cognition interleave visual landmarks with local directions between landmarks. Splitting annotation and modelling along these two parts makes crowdsourcing feasible and lets the agent ground each part in the right modality (landmark text to image, direction text to traversed path).
key_idea: Segment instructions into landmark and local-direction pieces, softly attend to one pair at a time with an ACT-LSTM indicator controller, and match landmarks to street-view images and directions to a rasterized top-view spatial memory of the path since the last landmark.
insight: Explicit 2D top-view memory beats no memory and a GPS-coordinate sequence. SPL is 6.87 with no memory, 9.04 with GPS memory and 11.92 with the map memory, and GPS degrades as trajectory length grows. Removing the indicator controller (9.71) or replacing ACT with a plain LSTM (8.95) also hurts. Cross-difficulty training shows models trained on harder (longer) routes transfer to easier ones but not vice versa. Performance drops roughly exponentially with landmark count, and the best 4-landmark SPL is only 11.92.
method: Talk2Nav dataset and annotation: 10,714 NYC routes on Google Street View. Landmarks are mined via submodular optimization (spread, near intersections, learned describability ranking). Annotators write separate landmark and sub-route direction descriptions, giving sub-unit correspondence.
Language segmentation: a BERT token classifier (91.4% accuracy) labels each token as landmark or direction and groups consecutive tokens into segments (L^j, D^j).
Soft dual attention: the reference position eta_t weights segments by exp(-|eta_t - j|) to give the current landmark and direction features. eta increments when the Indicator Controller fires.

Spatial memory: a 200x200 top-view image of the path since the last landmark, with adaptive scale starting at 5 m/pixel. It is re-initialized at each landmark, encoded by ResNet-101 and concatenated with the scale.

Matching modules: two transformer captioning models score the generative probability of the landmark text given the image and of the direction text given the memory image. The scores feed an ACT-LSTM Indicator Controller that outputs 0/1 for landmark reached, which also acts as an implicit stop.

Action module: two heads predict distributions over 9 actions (8 directions + stop), one from image+landmark and one from memory+direction. They are fused with weights predicted from the matching scores.
Training: supervised student-forcing with the next landmark as the target, cross-entropy plus weighted BCE for ACT. The matching nets are pretrained separately, then everything is trained end to end.

setting.backbone: ResNet-101 (ImageNet pretrained) + BERT + transformer captioning matchers + LSTM/ACT controller (trained on Talk2Nav)
setting.training_data: Talk2Nav train split (70% of 10,714 routes); BERT pretrained on BooksCorpus/Wikipedia; ResNet on ImageNet; 20,000 crowdsourced landmark-ranking pairs
setting.observation: 360° street-view panorama + top-view memory image of the traversed path + segmented instruction text
setting.action_space: 9 discrete actions: 8 headings at 45° steps (snapped to nearest road) + implicit stop via indicator controller
setting.simulator: Custom Google Street View city-graph simulator (NYC, 21,233 nodes)
setting.privileged: Traversed path for the memory image is computed from the simulated road network (odometry substitute); otherwise none

numbers.backbone: ResNet-101 + BERT + transformer matching + ACT IC
numbers.extra: 4-landmark routes; success threshold 100 m; trajectory budget 130% of GT length; greedy decoding
numbers.evidence: Table 1 (Comparison with prior s-o-t-a methods): Ours 11.92 / 633.85 / 42.2

numbers.backbone: ResNet-101 + BERT + transformer matching + ACT IC

numbers_note: Touchdown is not in the canonical list, so it is listed as 'Touchdown' as printed. The paper reports no SR. The Touchdown split is not explicitly named, so 'test' is assumed.
results: On Talk2Nav, the method reaches SPL 11.92 and NE 633.85 m, vs the best baseline Self-Monitoring at 9.56 and 740.12 m. Human SPL is 61.1, so much room remains. It also beats RConcat, Student-forcing and RPA on Touchdown (SPL 20.45) when trained only on Talk2Nav, and leads at every difficulty level from 1 to 4 landmarks.
limitations: Absolute performance on long routes is very low (SPL ~12 vs human 61), and only 4-landmark routes in a single NYC region are used.
Depends on a language segmenter (91.4% accuracy) whose errors cause failures, and on a simulated noise-free environment with path known from the road graph rather than real odometry.
Baselines lack landmark-level supervision, so the comparison is not fully equal; no real-robot experiments.
